**Marco, I’m sorry you’ve been hit by ransomware.** Below is a high‑level, end‑to‑end view of a typical ransomware campaign, the *defensive* signs you can watch for at each stage, and concrete actions a 12‑person firm can take to **detect early, contain quickly, and recover safely**. --- ## 1. Initial Access – How the attackers get in | What attackers usually do | Defensive signs to watch for | Immediate defensive actions you can take | |----------------------------|------------------------------|------------------------------------------| | • **Phishing / malicious attachments**
• **Credential stuffing / password spray** (e.g., RDP login attempts)
• **Exploiting un‑patched services** (e.g., VPN, Exchange, old SMB)
• **Supply‑chain compromise** (e.g., fake software updates) | • Unusual login times (e.g., 3 am from a new IP)
• Multiple failed logins on VPN/RDP/Office 365 → “Failed login” events (event ID 4625 on Windows)
• High‑volume spear‑phishing reports from staff
• New outbound connections to unfamiliar domains or IPs (from firewall/EDR logs) | • Enforce **MFA** on all remote access and cloud services
• Turn on **Office 365/Google Workspace** built‑in phishing/quarantine policies
• Enable **RDP/SSH hardening**: disable direct public access, limit to a jump‑host, use geo‑blocking
• Keep **security patches** current (use a patch‑management tool or service)
• Run a **phishing simulation** quarterly; train staff to report suspicious emails | --- ## 2. Reconnaissance – Mapping the environment | Typical attacker activity | Defensive signs | Mitigation | |----------------------------|----------------|-----------| | • Enumerate domain users, groups, computers, and shares (e.g., `net view`, PowerShell)
• Harvest service accounts, password hashes (Mimikatz‑style)
• Check backup & file‑share locations | • Spike in **authentication events** on domain controllers (e.g., event ID 4624 “Logon”)
• Unexpected **Kerberos TGT requests** from non‑admin accounts
• PowerShell execution logs showing `Get‑ChildItem`, `Get‑ADUser`, or credential enumeration (event ID 4103 / Sysmon) | • Implement **least‑privilege**; disable “Domain Admins” from being used on workstations
• Enable **account lockout** policies to blunt credential stuffing
• Use **group‑policy to block PowerShell v2** and limit allowed PowerShell execution paths
• Deploy **privileged access management (PAM)** for any admin accounts (even if you’re a small shop, there are lightweight SaaS options) | --- ## 3. Lateral Movement & Privilege Escalation – Moving through the network | Typical attacker activity | Defensive signs | Mitigation | |----------------------------|----------------|-----------| | • Use compromised admin credentials or pass‑the‑hash / pass‑the‑ticket
• Deploy remote management tools (PsExec, WinRM, SMB, RDP)
• Create new local admin accounts or scheduled tasks for persistence | • **SMB traffic** to unusual internal hosts (especially after business hours)
• Creation of **new scheduled tasks** or services with suspicious names (event ID 7045)
• Multiple **RDP sessions** from the same source IP
• **Unexpected Windows firewall rule changes** (event ID 2004/2005) | • Segment the network: place the file server and client workstations on separate VLANs (or at least a **firewall rule** that blocks workstation‑to‑workstation SMB)
• Enable **EDR/XDR** with behavior‑based detection that flags “mass SMB enumeration” or “multiple admin logins in short time”
• Turn off **SMBv1** (disable on all endpoints and the server)
• Restrict local admin rights: only give *local* admin to a dedicated service account, not to every user | --- ## 4. Data Collection & Exfiltration (optional but increasingly common) | Typical attacker activity | Defensive signs | Mitigation | |----------------------------|----------------|-----------| | • Copy client payroll files to a staging location (often on the same server)
• Transfer data to external cloud or C2 server (via FTP, Mega, custom C2) | • **Unusual outbound data volume** spikes (use your firewall/UTM’s traffic‑analytics)
• Connections to **new external IPs/domains** that are not part of normal business (e.g., *mass‑storage services*, *paste‑bin sites*)
• **Large file creation/modification events** on the file server outside normal hours (event ID 4663 on Windows) | • Enable **Data Loss Prevention (DLP)** or at least **file‑audit logging** on the file server (Windows “File Server Resource Manager” or a third‑party audit tool)
• Block outbound traffic to **unknown domains** via a DNS filter (e.g., Cisco Umbrella, OpenDNS)
• Schedule **automated backups** to an *offline* or *off‑site* location (see Recovery section) | --- ## 5. Encryption & Deployment | Typical attacker activity | Defensive signs | Mitigation | |----------------------------|----------------|-----------| | • Drop a ransomware binary (often a .exe, .dll, or .bat)
• Run it locally or remotely to encrypt files on the server and attached workstations
• Write a ransom note (e.g., `README.txt`, `DECRYPT_INSTRUCTIONS.html`) | • **Explosive file‑extension change** (e.g., `.locked`, `.encrypted`, `.vault`) on many files at once
• **Sudden loss of access** to network shares (error messages “Access denied” or “The directory is corrupted”)
• **New ransom‑note files** appearing on the desktop or in every folder
• **High CPU/memory usage** on endpoints during the encryption window (visible in Task Manager or EDR) | • **Immediate isolation** of infected machines: disconnect Ethernet/Wi‑Fi or pull the network cable (physically or via VLAN ACLs)
• Use your **EDR/XDR console** to “quarantine” the endpoint (prevents further execution)
• Verify that **your backups** are *immutable* and *offline* before you consider any payment (see Recovery) | --- ## 6. Extortion / Ransom Communication | Typical attacker activity | Defensive signs | Mitigation | |----------------------------|----------------|-----------| | • Send a ransom note via desktop wallpaper, email, or a drop‑site URL
• Threaten to release stolen data or increase ransom if not paid by a deadline | • Ransom note found on multiple machines or on the file server
• Email or HTTP request to a **new external domain** (often a `.onion` Tor link)
• Contact from the attacker (email, phone) demanding payment | • **Do NOT pay** (paying encourages more attacks and may be illegal under some jurisdictions).
• Preserve evidence: take photos, copy the ransom note, and note timestamps – they will be valuable for law‑enforcement.
• Report to **local law‑enforcement**, **FBI IC3**, or **CISA** (the more data they have, the better the chance of tracking the group). | --- ## 7. Containment & Recovery – Getting back to business | Phase | What to do | Tools & Tips for a 12‑person firm | |-------|------------|-----------------------------------| | **A. Verify your backups** | • Identify the *last known good* backup snapshot **before** the ransomware event.
• Ensure the backup is **immutable** (e.g., write‑once WORM storage, offline tapes, or a cloud bucket with version‑lock). | • If you use a cloud backup (Azure, AWS, Backblaze), confirm **Object Lock** or **Legal Hold** is enabled.
• Keep a copy of backups on an **air‑gapped drive** that is never attached to the network. | | **B. Rebuild / Reimage infected machines** | • Format and reinstall the OS on all compromised workstations and the file server (even if you think you cleaned them, you can’t be sure).
• Apply the latest OS patches before reconnecting to the network. | • Use a **standardized gold image** (e.g., a Windows 11 image with security hardening already baked in).
• For a small shop, consider a **re‑image service** (e.g., Microsoft Deployment Toolkit, or a local IT consultant). | | **C. Restore data** | • Mount the clean backup and restore only the needed payroll files.
• Run a **baseline integrity check** (hash or file‑size compare) to ensure you’re not reintroducing malicious payloads. | • Use a **file‑level backup** (e.g., Veeam Agent) that can restore individual folders.
• If you’re using **Windows Server Shadow Copy**, test the restoration process on a non‑production machine first. | | **D. Harden the environment before rejoining** | • Re‑apply security policies (GPO) that enforce:
 – PowerShell execution policy: *RemoteSigned* or *AllSigned*
 – SMBv1 disabled
 – UAC enabled, admin elevation prompts
 – Automatic updates enabled
• Install **EDR/XDR** (e.g., Microsoft Defender for Endpoint, SentinelOne, CrowdStrike – all have SMB‑friendly pricing). | • Run a **quick vulnerability scan** (e.g., using the free Qualys Community edition) before reconnecting to the internet.
• Enable **automatic alerting** for new admin logins, new services, and sudden file‑encryption activity. | | **E. Communicate** | • Notify your staff that the system is being rebuilt; provide a timeline for payroll processing.
• Prepare a brief “incident notice” for clients (if required by any compliance contract). | • Keep a **single source of truth** (a dedicated Teams channel) for status updates. | | **F. Post‑incident review** | • Document what happened, how it was discovered, which controls failed, and what was fixed.
• Update your **Incident Response Plan (IRP)** and run a tabletop exercise. | • Use a simple template (e.g., the NIST SP 800‑61r2 “IRP Checklist”).
• Schedule a **follow‑up training** session on phishing and password hygiene. | --- ## 8.
